title: Align & Stitch: inspect a real plan and verify the written mosaic
description: Run the current stitching interface on preserved real microscopy pixels, inspect the solved layout, write bounded image bands and verify both the mosaic and its coordinate records.
objectives: Distinguish this known-geometry crop example from an independently acquired tiled experiment.
Set grid, overlap, order and reference channel through the current GUI.
Inspect registration before writing and distinguish the band-buffer budget from total memory use.
Keep the stitched image, coordinate records and source provenance together.
prerequisite: For your own run, prepare tiles with known order, overlap and a useful registration channel; your counts and results will differ. The recording reuses nine preserved exact 800 × 800 × 4 crops from one real 2,000 × 2,000 × 4 field, with a 600-pixel step. These emulate a 3 × 3 acquisition, not nine independently acquired fields. The tutorial_A01 names are demonstration coordinates, not the original plate and well. Align & Stitch has no separate example-download button.

scenes.narration: Open Align and Stitch in Home's Tools category. Planning and writing are separate actions, so you can inspect a layout before creating its mosaic. This screen shows a tile layout and a textual report; the coloured rectangles are not a microscopy-image preview.

Choose the preserved tutorial tile folder. Its nine tiles are exact crops from one real four-channel image, deliberately arranged to emulate an acquisition with known geometry. They are not nine independent fields, and their tutorial plate and well names are demonstration identifiers.

Set a three-by-three grid, row-major order and overlap zero point two five. These eight-hundred-pixel tiles step by six hundred pixels. For your own data, use the actual acquisition order and nominal overlap; a serpentine scan must not be described as row-major.

Set reference channel one, the second plane in this zero-based example. Registration uses that plane's structure and applies one placement to all four channels. Choose a meaningful registration channel; this operation is not independent chromatic alignment of each channel.

Use minimum confidence zero point three, neighbour radius one and feather blending. Set the band-buffer budget to eight megabytes for this bounded example. That setting limits the writer's image bands; it does not cap every allocation or the application's total memory use.

Press Plan. All nine example tiles register, with no nominal-position fallback, and the proposed canvas is two thousand by two thousand pixels with four channels. No output image has been written yet. Inspect the registered, nominal and unplaced counts rather than treating any completed plan as acceptable.

Click the middle tile to inspect its coordinates, confidence, residual and contributing pairs. Here its origin is six hundred pixels in each direction, matching the known crop layout. Perfectly matching overlaps in this constructed example do not predict registration quality on a new acquisition.

Choose a new output folder and a separate coordinate database, leaving Overwrite off. Write stack is enabled only after a plan exists and a destination is supplied. Keep source tiles unchanged; assigning an output path is not a substitute for reviewing the registration.

Press Write stack. The actual output contains all nine tiles, and every pixel in all four channels matches the original field in this example. The result reports the output path and band-buffer use. This is a measured result for these known crops, not a promise of lossless registration for arbitrary images.

The coordinate database contains nine records. We check each source file, demonstration plate and well, field identifier, canvas position and output stack path, not just the row count. Preserve those records with the image and source manifest so downstream coordinates remain interpretable.

In Python, spacr.align.scan_tiles reads the tile layout and estimate_offsets builds the plan. write_stack creates the mosaic; save_coordinates and read_coordinates write and recover its coordinate table. The separate OPS workflow is not validated by this small stitch. Review real acquisition geometry before using either workflow for scientific conclusions.
